column2: The Board suspends the annuity payments to the Alberses for the summer; Dreier protests angrily (grossly unjust, a breach of the word given); Pittenger, usually mild, retorts sharply that Albers has almost sunk the ship by deserting the crew, all the more since he already has a post at the Cincinnati Art Academy and then Yale Albers's salary paid all summer although he is not teaching Consequences: Lasting resentment between former allies

To find the money, the college sells 70 acres to the Grove Stone Company; Pittenger negotiates the price upward from an initial offer of $22,500; some teachers think the price too low, all the more since it will later emerge that neighbors had merely leased their gravel rights while keeping the property $30,000 less a 10% agent's commission; Forbes agrees to maintain the mortgage on his terms and releases the gravel land for sale Consequences: The college survives financially

Surprisingly, serious consideration is given to recalling Rice, the only man reputed to be able to keep factionalism in check, all the more since he has just won the Harper centenary prize for his autobiography; through Pittenger, Aydelotte lets it be known that he thinks it a very bad idea The Harper 100th Anniversary prize for his autobiography Consequences: The candidacy abandoned

Social science students who had left in protest in the spring gradually come back, as do teachers: the Levis (he more reluctantly), Dehn full-time after a year of commuting from Wisconsin, Corkran back after an illness, Hazel Larsen (photography), the Jennerjahns (Color, Modern Dance), Joe Fiore (drawing, painting), Johanna Jalowetz (bookbinding, singing) The Rondthalers, tempted for a while, stay on their island of Ocracoke Consequences: The faculty partly reconstituted

Bodky, Trayer, and Pittenger (the last two themselves Quakers) recruit Quakers: McCandless (printing), Warrington (treasurer of a nonexistent office), Hetherington (harmony, solfège, introduction to music) and his wife Louise (piano), Turner (ceramics, once scorned by Albers as ashtray art) Turner, son of the Turner Construction Company, builds a marvelous kiln and inaugurates a distinguished tradition of pottery Consequences: A cultural conflict with the avant-garde

With a conservative regime taking over Olivet College, it is thought for a moment that a large group of dissident teachers and students will migrate together; only Leser, a distinguished anthropologist, and Shepard, a linguist, accept; both at once formal, academic, and independent, tough and eccentric Read “Flola Shepard” in the text; Shepard will become active in local civil rights causes Consequences: These rebels will last longer than the Quakers

Natasha writes that she has high hopes that next year will be a success thanks to the young students, the enthusiastic new teachers, and the veterans of the “civil wars,” to lead the college to a better destiny Consequences: Black Mountain has survived — no small feat
Albers and Dreier made their resignations final only once they were certain that Pittenger would take part in the reorganization; Albers had at one point tried to make Corkran rector.

Since his visit to Black Mountain in 1948, Cage has been to Paris, where he met Pierre Boulez, who introduced him to the work of Antonin Artaud; Cage passes Artaud on to David Tudor and Mary Caroline Richards. Consequences: The three often read Artaud together at Black Mountain; M.C. Richards becomes one of the first translators of Artaud into English

The Fuller-Goldowski correspondence of March 1949 (letters of March 16, 22, 31) leading to his return for the summer; in an interview (1969), Fuller speaks of the college's “small ambitions”. Consequences: Fuller returns in the summer of 1949
An exhibition of artist couples; Elaine will judge in retrospect that it belittled the women by “attaching” them to the real artists.

Elaine acts in Burckhardt's film The Dogwood Maiden and spends the summer in Provincetown, where Bill comes only once or twice; since 1944 the couple has been living in a cold-water flat on Carmine Street, after the sale of their building on 22nd Street.

After the financial failure of the Subjects of the Artist school (spring 1949), the artists rent a “club room” on Eighth Street and continue the Friday evening symposia; in the fall of 1949 the Club is founded, loosely affiliated with the Hans Hofmann School; it remains the epicenter of Abstract Expressionism throughout the 1950s. about twenty founding members, two of them women (Elaine de Kooning, Mercedes Matter) Consequences: the creation of the movement's social and intellectual center of gravity
The school fails financially and closes in the spring of 1949, pushing the artists to find their own meeting place. Consequences: the direct genesis of the Club

The article, illustrated with photos of Pollock painting his drip paintings, cigarette dangling, brow furrowed, fabricates the romantic image of the suffering, solitary existential artist; Pollock becomes a celebrity overnight. photos showing him with a dangling cigarette and a thoughtful frown Consequences: People who had never set foot in a gallery flock to his next exhibition at Betty Parsons's, buy, and invite Pollock and Lee Krasner to parties; the other artists want their share of celebrity.

Elaine describes Pollock's new paintings as violent in drawing and in the application of pigment but paradoxically quiet in expression; she praises the luminous networks of the large No. 1 and its range of whites, but concludes that the work is curiously uniform in its emotional content. 2 dollars earned per review; the money used to buy materials Consequences: She promotes what agrees with Bill's philosophy and disguises put-downs of what might compete with it

The dealer Sam Kootz commissions Harold Rosenberg to organize the exhibition Intrasubjectives, bringing together de Kooning, Baziotes, Gorky, Gottlieb, Graves, Hofmann, Motherwell, Pollock, Reinhardt, Rothko, Tobey, Tomlin.

Josef and Anni spend the summer in Mexico City, where Josef gives four seminars to architecture students; on their return they settle in New York. The exhibition of Anni's textiles at MoMA opens on September 13, 1949, organized by Philip Johnson and Edgar Kaufmann Jr.; first at Alex Reed's aunt's at 199 East 76th Street, then from October at 1245 Madison Avenue, the apartment of the painter Carl Holty. Consequences: A New York base for the Yale period.

At the end of September or early October, just before Albers leaves for Cincinnati, Kahn comes to discuss the plastics problem — probably their first meeting. Albers remembers showing there for the first time his new geometric line drawings, the future Structural Constellations. Geometric line drawings, investigations of impossible spatial structures. Consequences: The authors speculate on possible echoes between these drawings and Kahn's work.

During his six weeks of teaching at the Cincinnati Art Academy, Albers takes advantage of the nearby Formica Company, the leading manufacturer of laminated plastics, to engrave his Structural Constellations. Letter to Anni: “Friday I received my first engraving on laminated plastic. Pretty good, and much less expensive than in New York.” He plans to visit a laminated-plastics factory the next day. Consequences: He offers to talk to Formica about materials for Sawyer; Sawyer declines.

Kahn approaches Rohm and Haas (which introduced Plexiglas in the United States in 1936); the executive Edward Linforth, a 1938 Yale painting graduate, gladly supplies Plexiglas to the students. Plexiglas; Egbert Jacobson (Container Corporation of America) invited to the final jury. Consequences: The exhibition “Plastics in Art and in Industry” organized at the Yale University Art Gallery by Elliott Noyes.

Two weeks after the start, the first crit sessions; Kahn attends only the second day. An anonymous report: general confusion, a lack of initiative in handling the materials. Albers disappointed, confirmed in his conviction that there is no substitute for working directly with materials. Albers to Anni: “talking from 1.30 to 5.5” with the students and Switzer; almost all propose an immense “setting” for the plastic “without thinking of the plastic”; Kahn, the coordinator, absent — “We are wondering.” Materials handed out: sheets of various thicknesses, blocks, rods, cylinders. Consequences: Albers's disappointment; an unspoken divergence with Kahn over plastic.

Dreier openly carries on an affair with a woman teacher; the sexual double standard prevails, and moralists such as Trayer harshly condemn Dreier for making his wife suffer and taking advantage of the other woman. The woman's identity could not be established by the author. Consequences: Adds to the scandal of 1949; Perrow (in 2005) says he was not aware of affairs between teachers

Internal disagreements within the faculty make the post untenable for Josef as for Anni (who also taught there); they resign in 1949 Consequences: The following year, Albers is a visiting professor in Cincinnati, New York, Cambridge, then New Haven

Invited by his friend Walter Gropius to teach at the Harvard summer school, Albers gives the Busch-Reisinger Museum thirty-five of his photographs, with works in glass, prints, and typographic and wallpaper designs; the gift includes a copy of Die Koralle of April 30, 1930, with his photo of little Lilli Sachsenberg on the cover; several unmounted photographs bear agency stamps (dephot, Foto-Agentur Novofot), suggesting that he had sought to publish his Bauhaus photos in magazines 35 photographs; works in glass, prints, typography and wallpaper designs; dephot and Novofot agency stamps
Albers has recently resigned from Black Mountain College when Sawyer comes to sound him out in New York in 1950. Consequences: An opening toward Yale.

Albers asks Fuller to assemble a group of teachers for the summer: the painter Emerson Woelffer and his wife, the photographer Dina Woelffer; Nataraj Vashi and his wife Pra-Veena for Indian dance and philosophy; the couple Jano and John Walley for ceramics, jewelry, and the basic arts. All come from the Institute of Design in Chicago, a school founded by László Moholy-Nagy and largely modeled on the Bauhaus. three couples, all from the Institute of Design in Chicago
A retrospective exhibition in which she shows, among other things, the woven Room Dividers. Consequences: The structure of Minutiae will recall these weavings
Evelyn Bullock in costume for the costume party of the 1949 Summer Art Institute, photographed by Dina Woelffer.

Fuller authorizes Larsen to develop the Dymaxion principles, which she will use notably in her teaching through the modeling of tensegrity structures. models: tetrahedron, octahedron, icosahedron, vector equilibrium, close packing of spheres Consequences: She will teach the principles by which nature builds itself
A solo exhibition reviewed in the New York Times, earning her national recognition. a review in the New York Times

Fuller invites Emerson Woelffer, a teacher at the ID since 1942, formerly on the WPA (1938), then attracting national notice (the Whitney Annual, a first New York solo exhibition at the Artist's Gallery). His wife Dina, a photographer and student of Harry Callahan, also teaches that summer.

The students' interest and Charles Olson's support lead the college to invite the potter Robert Turner, trained at Alfred University, to inaugurate a pottery program. Albers, who resigned earlier in the year, had always opposed it, judging clay to lack rigor, mere ashtray art. Consequences: The birth of ceramics at BMC.

The pottery shop is designed and built by the architect Paul Williams in consultation with Turner, who conceives it as a production pottery. Turner notes that he was left alone, kept out of the college's divisive politics, busy with the construction of the shop and the kiln. Turner in fact lent the college the funds to build the pot shop (note 2)

Voulkos wins the 1949 Ceramic National at the Everson Museum while still an undergraduate at Montana State University; the prize earns him the direction of the Archie Bray Foundation, a fledgling residency in Helena. Before Black Mountain, he makes functional pottery with rich glazes, brushstrokes, and incised lines. Consequences: He will meet Hamada, Leach, and Yanagi there a few months after their visit to Black Mountain in 1952

Cage meets the French composer Pierre Boulez on a trip to Paris; Boulez was drawing on Artaud (notably in his Second Piano Sonata, 1948) to dismantle melodic and thematic conventions. Consequences: the first link in the chain leading to Artaud at Black Mountain

A summer course by Olson that the student Mark Hedden cites as starting a decisive turn away from literary drama toward a new concept of theater that Theater Piece No. 1 would accomplish three years later. Olson presents there “Wagadu,” a mythical narrative inspired by Soninke legends and taken from African Genesis (1937): a reading by Olson, music by Pete Jennerjahn, sets by Dan Rice; Olson describes it as a “jointure of speech-sound-motion, projection-melody-gesture”. a direct precedent for the nonlinearity of Theater Piece No. 1 Consequences: a preparation for Olson's “The Glyph Exchange”
Anni Albers becomes the first textile artist to have a solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Consequences: The following year, the Alberses move to New Haven, Connecticut.
A Paracas mummy bundle unwrapped in 1949 contained a fabric 11'3" wide; the textile is now in Lima. a fabric 11 feet 3 inches wide
A solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, then circulated across the United States for more than three and a half years. Length of the tour: more than three and a half years.

The former student Hazel Larsen Archer is appointed the college's first and only full-time teacher of photography; photography becomes a more permanent part of the course catalog. Consequences: Photography institutionalized at BMC, culminating in the 1951 summer institute.

Rauschenberg photographs the austere interior of the Quiet House: white stucco walls, two identical chairs in a corner, a diagonal band of light crossing one of the nine square windows a ray of light grazing the ear of the left-hand chair, a triangular shadow on the seat Consequences: Testifies to Archer's influence on his attention to light

MoMA and the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis organize a poster competition for vaccine research; 24 artists and photographers take part for a cash prize; first prize goes to Herbert Matter (two children skipping rope, captioned “One of them had polio–skilled teamwork brought recovery”) 24 participants, a cash prize; the reproduction of Archer's poster hung on the same wall as her photographs Consequences: A public reminder of Archer's own polio

MoMA acquires Andrew Wyeth's painting showing Christina Olson, stricken with polio, lying in a field, her back to the viewer, turned toward the house in the background Consequences: The most famous artistic depiction of a subject with polio

MoMA organizes a poster competition for polio research. First prize goes to Herbert Matter; Archer takes part and wins $500 for her submission. Dorothea Lange, invited, declines; Tana Hoban, Esther Bubley, and Margaret Bourke-White contribute. Matter's winning poster: two children skipping side by side, captioned “One of them had polio – skilled teamwork brought recovery”; Archer's poster: a photo of two young children in the center, “Don't be afraid” above, “Knowledge is a weapon against polio” below; Archer's prize: $500 Consequences: A miniaturized version of Archer's poster was pasted next to her photographs in the Steichen exhibition, linking the two

MoMA acquires Wyeth's painting (painted in 1948) showing Christina Olson, paraplegic after polio, lying in a field. Wyeth substituted for Christina's body the younger, able body of his wife Betsy. A remarkable coincidence: this acquisition, Archer's poster, and her photographs of Asawa and the Quiet House are all in MoMA's orbit in the same year. Christina propelled herself with her arms; her left hand and a lock of black hair point toward the house in the background Consequences: the painting makes the body a site for the production of social meaning

After Milwaukee State Teachers College and then Black Mountain College, Asawa, born in 1926 in Southern California, settles in San Francisco in 1949 and will live there until her death in 2013. Consequences: the beginning of her community of artist-mothers

Visiting her parents' temporary lodgings (a room in the former Japanese language school), Asawa deplores the uniformity of thousands of American houses: one house in five thinks alike because it is painted pink, and so on. Six people sleep in a room the size of Peggy's living room; “It is terrifying”

Before her arrival in San Francisco, Asawa collaborates with Tolk-Watkins on a collection of “poemstories”: black line drawings on white paper; for the poem about the six-striped tiger, she imagines vertical rows of postage stamps, the wavy lines of the postmark serving as makeshift legs. Black ink drawings on white paper; postage stamps and postmarks Consequences: A project probably left unfinished; Tolk-Watkins publishes Pigs Ate My Roses without Asawa's drawings

Tolk-Watkins confides her conflict between the roles of mother and artist and thanks Asawa for a frog (a jumping origami; it jumps admirably); Asawa encourages her to embrace motherhood without reservation. Quotations from both letters reproduced among the quotations

A summer 1949 wedding reception at Corbett's on Wolfback Ridge, facing the ocean and the bay. Asawa wears a black dress of fabric given by Anni Albers, sewn by Johanna Jalowetz (Trude Guermonprez's mother) as a suit with a long skirt that could be shortened after the ceremony. Charlotte Schlesinger plays the piano. Asawa has trouble reciting her vows; the baby Ragland Watkins crawls on the floor. A modest meal: cold cuts and champagne. A black dress of fabric from Anni Albers; a Dymaxion wedding ring designed by Fuller; cold cuts and champagne; the baby Ragland crawling on the floor; they were all laughing, and they were crying and laughing
Fuller designs the wedding ring, describing it in the same terms as his architectural experiments.

The couple settles in San Francisco, drawn by low rents and an affordable cost of living. Cheap rents; a single income could support a large family. Consequences: Settling in Noe Valley, the material condition for Asawa's future involvement in the schools.

Asawa writes to Albert Lanier: “There is no genius in my hands,” a phrase that sums up her rejection of modern artistic genius. Consequences: Becomes the title phrase of the conclusion of Troeller's book

Rauschenberg studies in Josef Albers's Bauhaus-inspired program at Black Mountain College; it is there that he begins to use collage. Consequences: The beginning of collage for Rauschenberg, leading to the collages of 1952 and then the combines.
Studies in the spring of 1949 with Josef Albers and his wife Anni; it is Albers's last year of teaching at Black Mountain, which his former students consider his best.

Rauschenberg takes up photography in the late 1940s during his stay at Black Mountain College; for a time he hesitates between painting and photography as a career before choosing both. Consequences: Photography becomes the cornerstone of his entire body of work

Susan Weil introduces Rauschenberg to the method of exposing light-sensitive blueprint paper to light, creating photographs without a camera. Life-size (1:1) silhouettes on a blue ground: Weil's hands gripping branches and twigs, feet, foliage, contorted bodies filling the paper to the edges, evoking the Vitruvian Man. Consequences: A series of blueprints, many of which do not survive.

During his first term at the Art Students League (fall 1949), Rauschenberg makes a now lost work consisting of collecting the footprints of his classmates on the school's threshold. Consequences: Anticipates Automobile Tire Print (1953).

A series of woodcuts among the first works to use seriality: the block is progressively scored with incised lines, the image passing from black to white in fourteen stages; one of the few works (apart from photographs) surviving from that year fourteen stages, from black to white, incisions in a woodblock

During his first term at the Art Students League in the fall of 1949, Rauschenberg collects the footprints of his fellow students crossing the school's threshold; a now lost work footprints on the school's threshold Consequences: Anticipates Automobile Tire Print (1953)

The real start of his career; his artistic vocabulary (sequences, grids, doublings, shimmerings, inversions, counterpoint between addition and subtraction, human scale) is established in the first four years.
His preoccupation with photography in 1949 arises from an inner conflict between curiosity and shyness: the camera serves him as a social shield, a license to observe.
Spends the summer at Susan Weil's family house; she introduces him to the method of exposing blueprint (cyanotype) paper. Consequences: A series of blueprints with Weil

The Club opens at the end of 1949; discussions take place there, notably on Zen Buddhism, which, according to Valerie Hellstein, feed a rhetoric of literalness and directness. Consequences: This rhetoric joins that of Cage and the critical discourse around Rauschenberg, contradicting the idea of a founding enmity between Cage and Abstract Expressionism.

Faced with falling GI enrollment and income, Dreier explores alternative plans (an art school with limited offerings), arousing resentment and distrust. When his resignation is requested, Dreier, the Alberses, Schlesinger, and Guermonprez resign at the end of the spring term. Consequences: Dreier is the last of the founders to leave; Natasha Goldowski and her colleagues recruit former students.

With no time to recruit, Goldowski and her colleagues call on former students: Fiore (painting), Warren “Pete” Jennerjahn (design), Hazel Larsen Archer (photography), Elizabeth Jennerjahn (dance); Richards and Levi return from sabbatical; Robert Turner, a fresh graduate of Alfred University, launches ceramics. Consequences: A generational renewal of the faculty.

When Josef Albers resigns in 1949, Fuller's electrifying presence earns him the offer of the vacant rectorship; he declines it. Consequences: He nevertheless returns in the summer of 1949 with a new dome

Summer 1949: Fuller returns with a freshly made prototype dome, more modest in size, of flexible metal tubing; the dome is successfully raised and an insulating plastic skin is tested. Photographed by Hazel Larsen Archer. Flexible metal tubing; a plastic skin Consequences: An experimental validation of tensegrity (“synergetic”)

Josef Albers resisted a ceramics course, judging clay too unruly for the students; a workshop is finally built under the aegis of Robert Turner, a young graduate of Alfred University. A studio 28 by 40 feet (about 8.5 × 12 m) in a flat field, beautiful light, good kilns and equipment. Consequences: The beginning of ceramics teaching, which lasts until the closing.

The completion of the Solís dam floods the site of Chupícuaro; it was thought that nothing more would be found there, but the tradition proves more widespread and discoveries continue. nearly 400 tombs with offerings were excavated there; dogs sometimes buried separately with offerings Consequences: Chupícuaro objects dispersed into collections

At the end of the summer of 1949, Dawson hands Olson a long, very bad poem about an existential lawnmower crossing the universe. Olson, embarrassed, does not know what to do with it and hands it back to the anxious student, who is hopping up and down. Dawson is nineteen, so anxious he cannot stand still Consequences: M.C. intervenes

She tells Olson that it is a poem Fielding wrote for him and asks whether he could not keep it and read it; Olson murmurs that he will. The poem no doubt soon came back to Dawson, who threw it away in his humiliation. M.C.'s voice takes on a hardness; Olson whispers “Yes, of course” Consequences: For Dawson, M.C. was a pal that evening

Olson talks about Paterson and the Cantos; Dawson, who had never heard of Williams or Pound, laughs out loud: “Bill Bill” and “Ezra Ounces”. Scattered smiles around the table, Olson annoyed. M.C. asks Olson to see it from the student's point of view: their names are funny.

Dawson describes Arnold, a Cuban painter, wonderful, very cultivated (painters, writers, politics), who reminds him of his brother-in-law Bill in his build and the way he slicks his hair back; he has not seen his work but is sure of his talent. hair slicked back, the same nose as Billy/Bill

From Dawson's first day, Hank expounds his communist ideas to him and does not budge an inch; he has read one or two books by Wolfe but speaks of him like an intimate and dares to tell Olson that he likes Wolfe “in places”. Hank thinks that believers in the Christian God are crazy or prissy; many students share this contempt.
Olson announces three pieces of fifteen minutes each: their version of the episode of the Cyclops and Ulysses in Homer's Odyssey; a selection from Ezra Pound; a free creation. three 15-minute pieces

Dawson takes painting, sculpture, Hindu philosophy, and French (over his head but wonderful), works on an oil painting, has made sketches of the teachers and students, and sends his mother a portrait of Buckminster Fuller. oil, sketches, a portrait of Fuller

During a discussion titled “A Desperate View...,” de Kooning speaks of the “void” on which God acts in Genesis: one can float in it, fly in it, be suspended in it, and, today, tremble in it; the idea of fitting into it is a desperate idea. He uses the word “tremble,” which becomes recurrent in his vocabulary from the 1940s on
September-October: shown with Elaine in “Artists: Man and Wife” at Janis's; a founding member of The Club, the artists' collective on East 8th Street.
For an exhibition at the Cincinnati Art Museum, Albers writes that without comparison and choice there is no value; and why fear that thinking and planning spoil the painting of a picture?

The culmination of Fuller's “total thinking” in the successful raising of a geodesic dome on the campus. Consequences: A touchstone of holistic planning applied to postwar housing, transportation, and communications
Albers asserts that progress does not depend on accidents alone: without order and control, one drowns or suffocates in chaos and decomposition.
The poet M. C. Richards stages works by Jean Cocteau, including Knights of the Round Table in 1949.
Masato Nakagawa photographs Buckminster Fuller with a model during the summer of 1949. a photograph preserved in the State Archives of North Carolina

Back on campus in 1949, Fuller successfully raises a self-supporting geodesic structure; he argues that the assembly of the dome is an essentially utopian project of “comprehensive anticipatory design science” A photograph by Masato Nakagawa showing Fuller with the model, summer 1949 (State Archives of North Carolina) Consequences: The dome becomes the emblem of his design revolution
Fuller writes to the media magnate that the reinspiration of the individual requires that artists become the capitalist bosses of the initial enterprise.

The following summer, Snelson shows Fuller a column about a foot high of wood and plastic: two equal wooden crosses oriented perpendicularly, the upper form suspended in the air by taut nylon threads, the lower serving as a prop — a principle of floating compression (discontinuous compression, continuous tension). Two wooden crosses of equal size; nylon threads; outer threads holding the exact right angle; 11½ × 5⅜ × 5⅜ inches according to the caption. Consequences: Fuller sees in it a new principle of efficient engineering.

Fuller asks Snelson for a modified version of X-Piece and later names the principle “tensegrity,” for tensional integrity; he declares that it will transform the building industry (very tall towers without buttresses or deep foundations). Each later patents his own version of the principle. A contraction of “tensional integrity”. Consequences: Separate patents by Fuller and Snelson; an implicit quarrel over authorship.

The transparent, double, heat-sealed, pneumatic plastic skin of a dome with a structure of thirty-one great circles (tubular beads and a continuous internal cable), designed and built at the Institute of Design in Chicago in 1948-49, is tested at Black Mountain during the summer of 1949. 31 great circles; tubular beads; a continuous internal cable; a heat-sealed double skin.

Fuller returns to the college in 1949 as director of the summer institute, accompanied by a dozen students from the Institute of Design in Chicago, bringing a new prototype dome influenced by Snelson's X-Piece. about a dozen ID students; a dome of flexible aluminum tubing with internal cabling, more modest than the venetian-blind model Consequences: The continuation of Fuller's “exploratory work” with enthusiastic students such as Snelson and Ruth Asawa.

The second dome, prepared months earlier for a demonstration at the Pentagon in Washington, is successfully raised at BMC, and a new insulating, transparent plastic skin, double, heat-welded, and pneumatic, is tested. a structure of flexible aluminum tubing with internal cabling; a double, heat-welded, pneumatic, transparent, insulating plastic skin Consequences: An experimental validation of the theory of tensegrity and of the “synergetic” process.

Fuller sets his students an apocalypse problem as an assignment: the city is evacuated, all residential and industrial concentrations of 50,000 people or more are in immediate danger of annihilation, consumer goods will be diverted to small decentralized communities, everything not decentralized will be destroyed. The assignment: “The city is to be evacuated… Everything not decentralized will be destroyed.”; a threshold of 50,000 people. Consequences: For Fuller, suburban dispersal was the optimal answer to the nuclear threat.

Hazel Larsen Archer photographs Buckminster Fuller with his dome at Black Mountain College in the summer of 1949 (fig. 3.17). Photograph preserved by the Estate of Hazel Larsen Archer and the Black Mountain College Museum + Arts Center.
In the summer of 1949, Fuller brings his secretary from the Institute of Design to transcribe his essay “Total Thinking” (written in 1949).

The Alberses move to New York; Anni becomes the first weaver to have a solo exhibition at MoMA. There she creates several open-slat blinds, light both visually and actually, with contrasts of texture and playful invention. The exhibition, well received, coincides with a newspaper strike and misses full public recognition. It includes wall hangings and fabric samples. open-slat blinds; a press strike
Leaves Black Mountain for New York; the first weaver to have a solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art The first solo exhibition of a weaver at MoMA

Facing an enormous deficit, Rector Albers and Treasurer Dreier proposed the unthinkable: a board of trustees. The rumor of an affair between the still-married Ted Dreier and a woman teacher fed the discord. At the end of the 1948-1949 year, the faculty asked for Ted Dreier's resignation and saw protest resignations by Albers and others. Ray Trayer and Natasha Goldowski, acting rector and secretary, proposed considering the return of John Andrew Rice, who had held the community together longer than anyone since. Frank Aydelotte wrote to his sister that nothing would be more disastrous. Rice never seriously pursued the idea. Aydelotte's letter of June 16, 1949 Consequences: Rice will say of the suggestion: “For a moment the clouds seemed to open.”

A year after Gorky's suicide, he firmly rejects the idea that Gorky had been under his influence: he is glad not to escape Gorky's powerful influence. the closing words: “Sweet Arshile, bless your dear heart”
A year after Gorky's suicide, de Kooning rejects, in an open letter to ARTnews, the idea that Gorky had been under his influence; he embraces Gorky's influence on himself.
